newsitem.title: USA: Cattle prices drop, gold and soybeans weaken.
newsitem.headline: Cattle prices drop, gold and soybeans weaken.

text.p: Cattle prices fell sharply on Monday on heavy selling triggered by a surprising government report on the size of the cattle herd and on concerns that consumer demand for beef may be hurt by a food safety scare.
At the Chicago Mercantile Exchange, live cattle for October delivery fell the allowable daily trading limit of 1.50 cents a pound to close at 68.70 cents.

In a monthly report issued on Friday, the U.S. Agriculture Department said placements of cattle onto feedlots in July in leading U.S. states were at 118 percent of the level of a year earlier, sharply above the average analyst guess of 106.5 percent.

"The Cattle-on-Feed was one of the most bearish reports we had in some time, with the placements up and well above trade expectations," said Karl Skold, director of research for Frontier Risk Management.
"I think we are still placing cattle in August, and the cattle that were placed in July were fairly heavy" in weight, more factors pointing to larger beef supplies this fall, he said.
Concern that consumers would shy away from beef or other meats after a recall of possibly tainted hamburger meat last week added to the bearish tone, livestock traders said.

The Agriculture Department on Friday said Hudson Foods Inc. of Rogers, Arkansas, recalled 1.2 million pounds of ground beef on suspicion of contamination by E.coli bacteria. Health officials blamed the beef and the microbe for 16 cases of illness in Colorado in July.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, heavy rains in the Midwest over the weekend spurred selling of soybeans as crop prospects in previously dry areas of southern Illinois improved.
Soybeans for September delivery closed 5-1/4 cents a bushel lower at $6.50-3/4.
"We're lower today on rain, but I don't think we're going to see a straight selloff until harvest when there's no longer a frost threat," said Paul Moravek, a trader with brokerage firm LIT.

After the market closed on Monday, the Agriculture Department indicated that recent rains had helped soybeans and corn. The amount of U.S. soybeans rated good-to-excellent rose two percentage points to 57 percent in the week ended Sunday. Corn at that level rose to 60 percent, also up two points.
Corn prices closed with slight gains on concern about this year's yields due to dry weather in July, along with rumors that China's crop losses from drought may be worse than expected.
September corn closed up 3/4 cent a bushel at $2.60-3/4.

In New York, precious metals ended sharply lower as the U.S. dollar and U.S. stocks and bonds recovered some ground. Traders said the gold market was also growing convinced that sales of bullion by producers or a European central bank were likely.
December gold at the COMEX closed down $4.80 an ounce at $324.70 after losing about $2.80 in the last half-hour alone.

"The stock market stabilizing today gave funds another opportunity to sell short, and some companies have been entering into new forward sales, given their financing arrangements and the low gold price," said analyst Ted Kempf with New York-based industry consultants CPM Group.
September silver ended down 5.8 cents at $4.502 an ounce, giving back some of Friday's 15.5 cent gain which took the contract to its highest level since early July.

At the New York Mercantile Exchange, gasoline led other oil markets lower. Gasoline had led the energy complex higher last week, largely on news of a couple of refinery production problems amid amid continued late summer demand. But some of those glitches were being worked out early this week, traders said.
September gasoline closed 1.37 cents a gallon lower at 65.44 cents, with September crude oil down 16 cents a barrel at $19.91 and September heating oil down 0.16 cent a gallon at 55.09 cents.
